cells.tense: Here, the pull of what might be felt runs through the practice and feeds it.
cells.act: reason it from first principles once
cells.ask: Follow one feeling you keep circling back to from the ground up, once — ten minutes at the usual chair, no fixing, just what actually follows.
cells.core:
You keep coming back to the same chair and the same shape, and under the repetition the pull of what might be felt is doing its work. The feelings aren't waiting until the practice is good; they're feeding it, and the work carries you toward what the heart hasn't met yet. That's the balance here. The chair is small, the pull is real, and they're on the same side.

Nothing needs choosing for a while. What's worth doing is following one of those feelings from first principles — not to solve it, just to see what actually comes of it. Ten minutes is enough. The rest can stay undecided. Work it through once and the pull quiets and the shape you've been training gets clearer.
cells.sheetLine: The pull feeds the practice instead of pulling away.
cells.verb: longing after what has not yet been felt
cells.place: a small room where you go back to the same thing until it shapes you

cells.tense: You keep reaching for the next possible feeling before the one in your hands has set.
cells.ask: Take what you're already gathering and keep it steady for seven days — no new opening, no next option — and notice what the week asks back.
cells.core:
The pull of what might be felt runs strong in you, and lately it's outrunning the practice. Every direction looks possible, so the one in your hands doesn't get finished; you're already imagining the next version of the feeling that hasn't arrived. Keeping one thing steady feels like losing the others. From the chair, it reads as a refusal to let a thing become what it already is.

Seven days is long enough to find out. Take what you're already gathering and keep it exactly as it is — no new opening, no next option — and do only what it needs. The other possibilities can wait outside. Some will lose their shine by Thursday; that's information. What stays, you keep.
cells.sheetLine: You keep the next feeling closer than the one you have.
cells.verb: longing after what has not yet been felt
cells.place: a small room where you go back to the same thing until it shapes you

cells.tense: The pull used to run through the practice, and now it stands at the door.
cells.act: let the mind rest instead of working the problem
cells.ask: Set the practice down for one hour and give thought nothing to work on. No count, no plan, no feeling you're supposed to arrive at by the end.
cells.core:
The pull of what might be felt was the current that carried you into the practice. It isn't carrying now. The work gets done anyway — steady, competent, quiet — and the feeders that used to bring feeling into it aren't reaching. The front of the room stands still.

Pushing harder into the practice won't bring the current back, and neither will forcing a feeling. What's starved here is the resting side, not the working side. Set it down for an hour and give thought nothing to work on. No count, no plan, no feeling you're supposed to have by the end. The pull comes back when there's room in the mind for it to land.
cells.sheetLine: The pull isn't reaching the practice that carried it.
cells.verb: longing after what has not yet been felt
cells.place: a small room where you go back to the same thing until it shapes you

cells.tense: The gathering is yours, and you'd call it the room, the mood, the moment.
cells.act: cut through the story to what actually follows
cells.ask: Go over three times you opened a room and take what you did down to what follows from it — then read those lines back as yours.
cells.core:
You are the one who gathers the possible feelings in your rooms — you open the ground for what might be felt, and you shape the practice so the room can hold it. You'd say it was going with the moment, the person's mood, the day. The shape you keep isn't. The gathering is done by someone, and the practice is carrying it, and you don't count yourself as the one doing it.

The pull belongs to the practice, and the practice belongs to you. Go back over three times you opened a room. Take what you did down to what actually follows — where you stood, what you said first, what you left alone. Three lines is enough. Read them back as yours, because they are. The hand that shaped the room was in the room.
cells.sheetLine: You gather the feeling and call it the room's.
cells.verb: longing after what has not yet been felt
cells.place: a small room where you go back to the same thing until it shapes you

The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is the closing turn about wanting every direction — cut from the draft; the core now names only what is available in the person's hands.
